boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's engagement at Ober-Hollabrunn (16 November 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: Murat's attack, with Lannes's and Soult's corps, on Bagration's Russian rearguard in its position behind Schöngrabern, from the late afternoon to eleven at night, and Walther's pursuit. The negotiations before it (the Austrian parley, Wintzingerode's convention and Napoleon's refusal of it), Kutusow's retreat on Pohrlitz and Bagration's junction with the army on the 17th are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 24,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry, 30,000 men, under Marshal Prince Murat, and side B (Russians and Austrians) 5,500 infantry, 1,500 cavalry and 12 guns under Lieutenant-General Prince Bagration, 7,000 men (our arithmetic). By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. His 30,000 for side A is more than the twenty-two thousand French who attacked in Victoires et conquêtes (claim victoires-side-a), and Schönhals gives no figure for the force engaged (claim schoenhals-side-a). His 7,000 for side B is near the six thousand of both other accounts (claims victoires-side-b and schoenhals-side-b); his 12 guns equal the twelve guns Victoires has side A take (claim side-b-losses-reported), and neither other account gives side B's guns before the engagement. His infantry and cavalry figures are not in the passages read. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'victory of the French (24,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry = 30,000 men) under Marshal Prince Murat over the Russians and Austrians (5,500 infantry, 1,500 cavalry, 12 guns) under Lieutenant-General Prince Bagration'.

claims.value: Side B in Victoires et conquêtes: the Russians had taken position behind the village of Schoen Grabern, beyond a defile defended by six thousand men of their best troops; the six thousand Russians who fought at Guntersdorf were the rearguard under Prince Bagration. Victoires names only Russians in the combat. Before the engagement, it says (OCR), an Austrian officer came as a parlementaire and asked that the Emperor of Germany's troops be allowed to separate from the Russians, and Murat consented.
claims.rationale: Side A's compilation on side B, read from the page images except the Austrian parley (OCR). Victoires does not say whether the Austrian troops did separate or whether any fought at Guntersdorf; Schönhals has the Hessen-Homburg hussars of Nostitz's brigade distinguish themselves in the fight (claim schoenhals-side-b), and Bodart has Russians and Austrians (claim bodart-strength). The rearguard was the force Bagration commanded, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'the Russians had taken position behind the village of Schoen Grabern, beyond a defile, defended by six thousand men of their best troops'; 'the six thousand Russians who had just fought at Guntersdorf had shown themselves such as the great Frederick had depicted them, when he said that it was not enough to kill a Russian soldier, one still had to push him to make him fall'; 'Murat, by the emperor's orders, gave notice of the breaking of the armistice he had provisionally granted to Prince Bagration, commanding the rearguard of the Russian army'; 'Murat and Marshal Lannes intended to follow up this advantage and had made their dispositions accordingly, when an Austrian officer came forward as a parlementaire and asked that the troops of the Emperor of Germany be allowed to separate' (p. 211) 'from the Russians. Murat consented to it, reflecting that this act of condescension on his part might lead the Austrian monarch to sue for peace sooner' (p. 212) (OCR).

claims.value: Side B in Schönhals, its own account: Bagration stayed behind at Schöngrabern with a rearguard of 6000 men to cover the retreat, and Murat attacked the 6000 Russians; of Nostitz's brigade the Hessen-Homburg hussar regiment distinguished itself above all and suffered very much. claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. Schönhals does not say whether the 6000 included Nostitz's brigade or how many of it fought; the hussars of Nostitz's brigade are Austrian, as Bodart's 'Russians and Austrians' imply (claim bodart-strength), while Victoires names only Russians (claim victoires-side-b). claims.value: Murat commanded side A and decided the attack; Napoleon refused the convention Murat had accepted and hastened his troops forward. Victoires: Murat accepted Wintzingerode's capitulation and had Belliard, his chief of staff, settle and sign it (OCR); Napoleon did not approve it, judging Wintzingerode not authorised to conclude it (OCR); by the emperor's orders Murat gave notice of the breaking of the armistice; on the 16th Murat, with his usual impetuosity, wanted to attack the defile at once though night had fallen, and Soult advised against a night action in vain; after cavalry skirmishes Lannes sent Oudinot's grenadier division to attack the position in front and on the left, Soult turned it on the right with Legrand's division, and Vandamme's division supported the grenadiers. Schönhals: Murat halted his troops and Winzingerode concluded a kind of convention with him; Napoleon, seeing through the Russians' ruse, refused to confirm it, hastened the IV Corps' march, ordered his Guard to Hollabrunn and Caffarelli's division of the III Corps to Znaym, and left Schönbrunn himself; at dusk Murat had Oudinot's grenadier division advance in two columns against the Russians' centre and right wing, Suchet was to turn their left, Legrand's division was formed in two columns against it, one to attack it, the other to cut the road beyond Grund, and Vandamme followed in reserve.
claims.rationale: Side A's decisions as both accounts give them, read from the page images except Victoires's account of the capitulation and its refusal (p. 212, OCR). The two accounts agree on the attack's commander and its dispositions; Victoires puts Lannes and Soult between Murat and the divisions, and has Soult advise against the attack. English renderings (ours): Victoires, 'such a proposal seemed too much in the army's interest for Murat not to accept it on the spot'; 'General Belliard, the prince's chief of staff, was therefore charged by him to settle the articles of this capitulation with Baron Wintzingerode, and in the evening these two generals settled and signed at Hollabrunn a capitulation by which Prince Murat consented to suspend his march on Moravia, and the Russian army undertook to leave Germany at once, withdrawing by the road it had taken to come there'; 'Murat sent this capitulation to the Emperor Napoleon, who did not approve it, because, this act being a kind of treaty, he did not think Baron Wintzingerode sufficiently authorised to conclude it' (OCR); as in claim victoires-side-b for the breaking of the armistice; as in claim hollabrunn-ground for the 16th; 'Murat, with his usual impetuosity, wanted to attack this defile at once, although the day had already fallen'; 'Marshal Soult advised not to engage an action by night, in which dispositions are uncertain, mistakes frequent and the results often fatal to the assailants: his entreaties were useless, Murat ordered the attack'; 'the action began with some cavalry skirmishes, after which Marshal Lannes sent forward the division of Oudinot's grenadiers to attack the enemy's position in front and on the left, while Marshal Soult had it turned on the right by the division Legrand, while the division Vandamme supported that of the grenadiers'; Schönhals, 'Murat fell completely into the trap laid for him, he had his troops halt, and Winzingerode even concluded a kind of convention with him, which was sent to Napoleon at Schönbrunn for confirmation'; 'Napoleon, seeing through the Russians' ruse, refused his confirmation to the convention concluded, for which he declared General Winzingerode not furnished with full powers, and hastened the march of the IV Corps, which followed Murat's; at the same time he ordered his Guards to set out for Hollabrunn and the division Caffarelli of the III Corps to march to Znaym; he himself left Schönbrunn at once'; 'at dusk Murat had the grenadier division Oudinot advance in two columns against the centre and the right wing of the Russians'; 'Suchet was to turn their left'; 'against the latter the division Legrand was also formed in two columns, the one for a direct attack on it, the other to cut the road for it beyond Grund'; 'Vandamme followed as reserve'.

claims.value: Bagration commanded side B's rearguard. In Schönhals, when Bagration discovered the danger, he sent the Emperor's adjutant-general, Prince Dolgorucky, to Murat, repaying ruse with ruse, and opened to him the prospect of a separate peace with Russia, a hope Kutusow had General Winzingerode feed; Kutusow gained time thereby to reach Lechwitz with his main body in the night before the 16th, and Bagration stayed behind at Schöngrabern with a rearguard of 6000 men to cover the retreat; Bagration had taken an advantageous position behind Schöngrabern, beyond the defile of the village of Grund, and the Russians kept up the fight with unexampled bravery until 11 at night. In Victoires, Baron Wintzingerode, aide-de-camp general of the Emperor of Russia, came to the French outposts and asked to capitulate for the Russian army (OCR), and Napoleon regarded the step as a ruse of the Russian commander-in-chief to gain time (OCR); Bagration used the four hours' notice to hasten his retreat, and the Russians, with the advantage of the position, received the attack vigorously; their long resistance let the Russian army continue its retreat.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions as both accounts give them, read from the page images except Victoires's sentences on Wintzingerode (p. 212, OCR). The accounts differ on who began the deceptions (claim armistice-ruse). Kutusow, the army commander, chose to leave the rearguard; Bagration commanded it and, in Schönhals, sent Dolgorucky, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Schönhals, 'when Bagration discovered the danger facing him, he sent, repaying ruse with ruse, the Emperor's adjutant-general, Prince Dolgorucky, to Murat and opened to him the prospect of' (p. 137) 'a separate peace with Russia. Kutusow had this hope fed by General Winzingerode' (p. 138); 'Kutusow thereby gained time to come to Lechwitz with his main body in the night before the 16th; on the 17th he reached Pohrlitz on the Brünn road'; as in claim schoenhals-side-b for the rearguard; 'Bagration had taken an advantageous position behind Schöngrabern, beyond the defile of the village of Grund'; 'a murderous fight developed, which was kept up on the Russians' side with unexampled bravery until 11 o'clock at night'; Victoires, 'some moments later Baron Wintzingerode, aide-de-camp general of the Emperor of Russia, presented himself at the French outposts and asked to capitulate for the Russian army' (OCR); 'at bottom the French emperor regarded Baron Wintzingerode's step as a ruse of the Russian commander-in-chief to gain time and receive the reinforcements that were advancing from upper Moravia' (OCR); as in claim victoires-side-b for the four hours; 'General Oudinot, at the head of the brigade of grenadiers commanded by General Laplanche-Mortière, fell on the Russians with his accustomed dash; but these, who had the advantage of the position, received the shock vigorously'; 'their long resistance allowed the Russian army to continue its retreat'.

claims.value: The two accounts disagree on who deceived whom before the engagement. Victoires (OCR): an Austrian officer came as a parlementaire and asked that the Austrian troops be allowed to separate from the Russians, and Murat consented, hoping the Austrian monarch would sue for peace sooner; then Wintzingerode asked to capitulate for the Russian army, Murat accepted, and the capitulation was signed, to be carried out only after Napoleon's ratification, the Russian army and the French corps meanwhile keeping their positions and giving four hours' notice before reopening hostilities; Victoires quotes the official bulletin on the Frenchman's thoughtless generosity out of action. Schönhals: Murat, not daring to attack Kutusow's 32.000 in front, took refuge once more in deceit, engaged General Nostitz, who held the furthest outposts, in conversation and assured him of an armistice already in force and an early peace with Austria, and during the conversation turned Nostitz and the flank of the Russian rearguard; Bagration answered ruse with ruse, and Murat fell completely into the trap.
claims.rationale: Both accounts as read: Victoires in the OCR (pp. 211-212) except the four hours' notice, which its p. 213 repeats on the page image; Schönhals on the page images. They are opposed on the Nostitz episode (an Austrian request to separate that Murat granted, against a deception of Nostitz by Murat) and agree that Wintzingerode concluded the convention that Napoleon refused. Each account's deception is a decision of a commander before the engagement, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): as in claims victoires-side-b, side-a-command and side-b-command; Victoires, 'these conditions were to be carried out only after the ratification of the Emperor Napoleon, and meanwhile the Russian army and the ... (OCR) French corps were to stay in the positions they held: in case of non-acceptance by the French monarch, each side was to warn the other four hours before resuming hostilities' (OCR); 'one must recognise here, says the editor of the official Bulletin on this subject, the character of the Frenchman, who, brave in the fray, is often of a thoughtless generosity out of action' (footnote, OCR); Schönhals, as in claim schoenhals-side-b for Murat's deceit; 'at the sight of them Murat entered into a conversation with Nostitz and gave him too the assurance of an armistice already in force and of an early peace with Austria, which pretences he sought to confirm by his undisturbed march up to this point'; 'during this conversation he turned not only Nostitz but also the flank of the Russian rearguard, standing somewhat further back, and threatened even that of the main army'.

claims.value: Bodart records a victory of side A (French) under Marshal Prince Murat over side B (Russians and Austrians) under Lieutenant-General Prince Bagration on 16 November. Victoires: after a stubborn combat that lasted until eleven at night the French were masters of the battlefield, and the Russians' long resistance allowed the Russian army to continue its retreat; General Walther pursued the Russians with a brigade of dragoons. Schönhals: the Russians kept up the fight with unexampled bravery until 11 at night; Bagration reached Lechwitz at noon on the 17th, where the Austrian General Caramelli received him with two cuirassier regiments, and was at Frainspitz by evening, an hour from the army; through Kutusow's fortunate arrival at Pohrlitz and Bagration's steadfastness the union with the 13.000-strong Austrian corps was achieved.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A won), read from Bodart's entry, with the other accounts' ending, read from the page images. Victoires gives side A the field; Schönhals does not say who held it, and dwells on the rearguard's success in covering the army's retreat and junction, which concerns the campaign, not the tactical result, and is his judgment, not a measured effect. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; '1805 16/11. engagement at Ober-Hollabrunn (4.)'; Victoires, 'finally, after a stubborn combat that had lasted until eleven in the evening, the French found themselves masters of the battlefield, of eighteen hundred prisoners, of twelve guns and of a hundred and some baggage wagons'; as in claim side-b-command for the long resistance; 'General Walther, at the head of one of his brigades of' (p. 214) 'dragoons, pursued the Russians and took another three hundred prisoners from them' (p. 215); Schönhals, as in claim side-b-command for the fight; 'Bagration reached Lechwitz at noon on the 17th, where the Austrian General Caramelli received him with two cuirassier regiments'; 'in the evening he already stood at Frainspitz, an hour from the army'; 'through Kutusow's fortunate arrival at Pohrlitz and Bagration's steadfastness the union with the 13.000-man-strong Austrian corps was achieved, which on this day FML Prince Liechtenstein commanded instead of Auersperg'.

claims.value: Bodart describes Ober-Hollabrunn as a market town in Lower Austria, 42 km north-west of Vienna. Victoires puts the encounter before Hollabrunn, near the village of Guntersdorf, with the Russians in position behind the village of Schoen Grabern, beyond a defile, with the advantage of the position; the village, set on fire by Russian shells from the start, lit the French position, and the wind drove thick smoke that hid the Russians' movements (OCR); the attack began after nightfall and the fight lasted until eleven at night. Schönhals puts Bagration's advantageous position behind Schöngrabern, beyond the defile of the village of Grund, has Legrand's second column sent to cut the road beyond Grund, and has the burning Schöngrabern light the battlefield.
claims.rationale: Ground, light and smoke from Bodart's location and the two accounts, read from the page images except Victoires's sentences on the fire and the wind (pp. 213-214, OCR); no map was inspected. The position was the ground Bagration had taken, and the night and the fire came with the hour Murat chose and Russian shells; the claim is tagged inherited for the ground. English renderings (ours): Bodart, 'market town in Lower Austria, 42 km north-west of Vienna'; Victoires, 'Murat himself set out, and on 16 November at four in the afternoon the French troops found themselves in the presence of the Russians before Hollabrunn, near the village of Guntersdorf'; as in claim victoires-side-b for the defile; as in claim side-b-command for the advantage of the position; 'their shells having set fire to the village of Schoen Grabern from the beginning of the action, the fire' (p. 213) 'soon showed itself in a frightful way and did much harm to the French troops, whose position it lit; the wind, driving great clouds of a thick and fetid smoke, prevented the Russians' movements from being made out' (p. 214) (OCR); as in claims side-a-command and bodart-winner for nightfall and the hour; Schönhals, as in claims side-b-command and side-a-command; 'Schöngrabern, set on fire by Russian shells, lit the battlefield'.

open_questions: Deferred: the official bulletin that Victoires cites on the Austrian parley (footnote, OCR), Murat's and Lannes's reports and any French return of the 4th and 5th corps and the cavalry reserve for mid-November, none inspected; Russian accounts of the rearguard action, which neither account cites in the passages read; Alombert and Colin's t. IV, which ends with Saint-Pölten and Krems before this engagement (its OCR has no hit for Hollabrunn); Victoires's text from p. 209 to the selected section (the entry into Vienna and the crossing of the Danube), read and not cited; Völderndorff's brief account of Hollabrunn (OCR, pp. 278-279 by its page heads), a fourth family read in the follow-up for Steken and not cited, which gives a strength for Bagration's rearguard. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: Victoires's date for Lannes's arrival at Hollabrunn, the brigades of light cavalry at its head, the wagons taken at that arrival and the number of French corps named in the capitulation's conditions; the page numbers of Victoires's OCR quotes, read from the OCR running heads.

Most consequential gap: side A's engaged strength. Bodart gives 30,000 (24,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry), Victoires twenty-two thousand French who attacked, and Schönhals no figure for the force engaged, only the 50.000 Murat led across the Danube on the 13th. The targeted follow-up read the passages around every hit for Hollabrunn, Schöngrabern and Guntersdorf, with their OCR variants, in both parents (the summaries of the volume's chapter, Napoleon's proclamation on the eve of Austerlitz, and Schönhals's narrative of 17-18 November and table of contents, none of them cited) and found no other figure for side A's force. A return of the 4th and 5th corps and the cavalry reserve for mid-November could close it.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side A's strength (Bodart 30,000; Victoires twenty-two thousand attacking; Schönhals none); side B's composition and strength (Bodart 5,500 infantry and 1,500 cavalry, Russians and Austrians, 7,000 by our arithmetic; Victoires six thousand Russians, the Austrians having been allowed to separate before the engagement, OCR; Schönhals 6000 Russians, with the Hessen-Homburg hussars of Nostitz's brigade in the fight); the deceptions before the engagement (Victoires, OCR: an Austrian request to separate that Murat granted; Schönhals: Murat's deceit of Nostitz, answered by Bagration's and Kutusow's ruse); side B's prisoners (Bodart 1,800; Victoires eighteen hundred and three hundred more in the pursuit); side A's loss (Bodart about 2,000; Schönhals considerable, above all the French; Victoires names wounded generals and officers, no number). The accounts agree on the date, the hour, Murat's command, the divisions engaged, the burning village and the end of the fight at eleven at night.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 1,800 prisoners and 12 guns equal Victoires's figures, and his 30,000 for side A and his infantry and cavalry for side B are not in the passages read); Victoires et conquêtes, t. XV (the French compilation of 1819; in this section it cites the official bulletin by name, OCR, and how far its narrative depends on the bulletins was not checked); Schönhals (the Austrian account written in 1831 and printed in 1873, which by its preface draws what it says of the French army's operations from that army's bulletins, not inspected, so the two may share the bulletins for side A; on side B and the deceptions they differ).
